title: On service
hook: he warns against service mixed with pride

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hundred moons and a thousand suns, and still darkness without the Guru. Your line was the guru as light. Whose light did you give thanks for? Day one thousand one hundred seventy-nine.

A bundle of grass, cut for the cattle, still soaking wet and caked with mud. Someone has to carry it home on their head. In the story Sikhs tell, Guru Nanak asks who will take it. His sons have reasons not to. Then a newer disciple steps up, a man named Lehna, dressed in fine clothes, and lifts the dripping bundle onto his own head. Mud runs down his face and into the cloth. He carries it anyway. Lehna is the man who would become Guru Angad. And when he later wrote about service, he didn't praise big gestures. He warned about a quieter danger, the one that can ride along on top of any good deed.
screen: `A BUNDLE OF WET GRASS.` → `LEHNA LIFTS IT.` → `A QUIETER DANGER.`

segments.voice: In Asa di Var, the morning ballad, there's a salok marked Mahala two, Guru Angad's voice. Here it is in paraphrase. A servant who does his service with pride, and argues while he does it, and talks on and on, does not win the Master's favor. But one who loses himself and serves, that one is given some honor. Nanak, he meets the One he is devoted to, and his devotion is accepted. Look at the three things the salok names. Pride. Arguing. Talking too much. None of them stop the work. The servant in the first half is still serving. The dishes still get washed, the floor still gets swept. The problem isn't the work. It's what rides along on top of it. Pride says, look who's helping. Arguing says, I'd do it differently and you should know. Talking says, let me tell you how much this cost me. Each one turns service back toward the self. And the second half is plain. Lose yourself and serve. Not lose the work, lose the self in it. Then honor comes, the salok says, not from the people watching but from the Master. In Sikh life, this is seva, selfless service: cooking and serving langar, washing dishes, cleaning shoes at the gurdwara door. The Lehna story fits the salok exactly. He didn't make a speech about the muddy grass. He didn't mention his ruined clothes. He just carried it. That's what Guru Angad asks of service: do it, and leave yourself out of it. That's today's line.
screen: `PRIDE, ARGUING, TOO MUCH TALK.` · `THE WORK STILL GETS DONE.` · `LOSE YOURSELF AND SERVE.` · `HE JUST CARRIED IT.` · then, large: `SERVE PLAINLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: serve without pride. In the sit, let the breath slow. Think of one small service you'll do today, for family, a coworker, a stranger. Picture yourself doing it. Now notice which of the three would most like to come along: the pride, the arguing, or the telling everyone about it afterward. Don't scold it. Just see it, and picture setting it down at the door before you go in. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
On service. Guru Angad's warning: service done with pride, arguing and too much talk loses its way; lose yourself and serve, and it is accepted. Today's word.
Your line: serve plainly. Do one helpful thing today and tell no one, not even a hint. Day one thousand one hundred seventy-nine.

howItsDone: Sikhs practice seva, selfless service, in the gurdwara and beyond: cooking and serving langar, washing dishes, cleaning, and looking after the shoes of the sangat, ideally without seeking notice.

myth: in the salok, the proud servant stops doing the work
the work still gets done; the problem is the pride, arguing and talk riding on top of it.
the salok says the one who loses himself and serves is given honor
and his devotion is accepted, it says.
Lehna, in the story, is the man who became Guru Angad
the disciple who carried the muddy bundle later became the second Guru.

fork.setup: you're in your best clothes. your teacher asks who will carry a dripping bundle of muddy grass home on their head. what does Lehna do?
options: lifts it onto his own head and carries it.
carries it, then points out his ruined clothes.
fork.reveal: the story says he carried it, mud running down, and said nothing about the clothes: service with the self left out.

original.note: seva: selfless service, the work Guru Angad's salok asks to be done without pride.

trapdoor: what you thought: service is good as long as the work gets done.
what it means: the salok warns that pride, arguing and talk can ride on top of service and spoil it.
what a scholar hears: a Mahala two salok in Asa di Var: lose yourself and serve, and the devotion is accepted.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Asa di Var, salok Mahala 2, Ang 474 (the servant who serves with pride and argument; lose yourself and serve)
